On the integrality of étale extensions of polynomial rings

Lázaro Orlando Rodríguez Díaz Address: Instituto de Matemática, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, RJ, Brazil. Email address: lazarord@im.ufrj.br
Abstract.

Motivated by a valuation theorem, recently obtained by Rangachev, we study the étale extensions A⊂BA\subset B of polynomial rings over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, such that the integral closure A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB. We prove that in this case A¯\overline{A} has infinite cyclic divisor class group, where the generator is a prime divisor equal to the complement of Spec​(B)\textrm{Spec}(B) in Spec​(A¯)\textrm{Spec}(\overline{A}). Moreover, this prime divisor coincides with the ramification divisor of the finite extension A⊂A¯A\subset\overline{A}. In this situation we carry out Wright’s geometric approach for two-dimensional non-integral étale extensions. It follows from the work of Miyanishi that Spec​(A¯)\textrm{Spec}(\overline{A}) is a smooth affine surface. We show that Spec​(A¯)\textrm{Spec}(\overline{A}) is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, more precisely a Danilov-Gizatullin surface of index three. Based on Wright’s analysis of which of these affine surfaces can factorize an étale morphism of the complex affine plane and his description of its affine coordinate rings, we prove that under the strong assumption that A¯\overline{A} is always a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB, any two-dimensional complex étale extension is integral.

1. Introduction

The problem we want to address is the following: how far is the integral closure A¯\overline{A} of AA from BB, assuming that an A=k⁡[y1,…,yn]⊂B=k⁡[x1,…,xn]A=k[{y}_{1},\,\ldots,\,{y}_{n}]\subset B=k[{x}_{1},\,\ldots,\,{x}_{n}] is an étale extension of polynomial rings over an algebraically closed field kk of characteristic zero? It is well-known that, if BB is integral over AA then B=AB=A, [16, Theorem 47], [17, Theorem 3.3]. Then the problem considered makes sense. On the other hand, it is known that the integral closure of AA in Frac⁡(B)\mathrm{Frac(B)} is the intersection A¯=∩𝒱\overline{A}=\cap\mathcal{V} of the family of valuations rings 𝒱\mathcal{V} of Frac⁡(B)\mathrm{Frac(B)} that contains AA, [5, Theorem 19.8]. Therefore, we can write A¯=B∩(∩𝒱)\overline{A}=B\cap\left(\cap\mathcal{V}\right), where the intersection is taken over all valuations rings 𝒱\mathcal{V} of Frac⁡(B)\mathrm{Frac}(B) that contain AA and does not contain BB. The question can be reformulated as: how many valuations rings are there?, can we describe them?

Recently, Rangachev [14] proved that if A⊂BA\subset B are integral domains, AA is Noetherian and BB is a finitely generated AA-algebra then there are a finite number of uniquely determined discrete valuation rings 𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i} each of which is a localization of A¯\overline{A} at a height one prime ideal, that is, A¯=B∩(∩i=1r𝒱i)\overline{A}=B\cap\left(\cap_{i=1}^{r}\mathcal{V}_{i}\right), 𝒱i=A¯𝔭i\mathcal{V}_{i}=\overline{A}_{\mathfrak{p}_{i}}, ht⁡(𝔭i)=1\mathrm{ht}(\mathfrak{p}_{i})=1. In the present work we study the simplest possible case, that is, we assume that there is only one discrete valuation ring in the above decomposition, A¯=B∩A¯𝔭\overline{A}=B\cap\overline{A}_{\mathfrak{p}}. Due to Rangachev’s results this is equivalent to assume that A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB, see Lemma 2.3.

We prove in Proposition 2.4 that if A=k⁡[y1,…,yn]⊂B=k⁡[x1,…,xn]A=k[{y}_{1},\,\ldots,\,{y}_{n}]\subset B=k[{x}_{1},\,\ldots,\,{x}_{n}] is an étale extension of polynomial rings over an algebraically closed field kk of characteristic zero, such that A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B and A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB, then Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)=V⁡(𝔭)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B)=V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right), where 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is a prime ideal of height one in A¯\overline{A}, and the divisor class group Cl⁡(Spec⁡(A¯))≅ℤ≅⟨V⁡(𝔭)⟩\mathrm{Cl}(\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}))\cong\mathbb{Z}\cong\left\langle V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right)\right\rangle. Moreover, the prime divisor V⁡(𝔭)V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right) coincides with the ramification divisor of the finite extension A⊂A¯A\subset\overline{A}, see Corollary 2.5.

In Section 3 we apply this proposition to carry out Wright’s geometric approach [18] for two-dimensional non-integral étale extensions. Wright proved that, given an étale extension A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y] (that satisfies some assumptions, see Remark 3.4) such that A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B, then we can construct a normal affine variety VV, containing Spec​(B)\textrm{Spec}(B) as an open subvariety, such that VV admits a map to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} making it an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle except over one point of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} whose fiber is V∖Spec​(B)V\setminus\textrm{Spec}(B) set-theoretically. We proved that if A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB the obstacles encountered by Wright to prove that VV is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} can be surpassed. The difficulties are: Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) could have singularities, and even if it did not have any singularities, the fiber at infinity may be non-reduced. Due to Miyanishi’s work, Proposition 2.4 implies that Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is a smooth surface, see Proposition 3.3. We proved the following result:

Theorem.

Let A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y] be an étale extension such that A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B and A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB, then Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is a smooth affine surface that admits the structure of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, π:Spec⁡(A¯)→ℙ1\pi:\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\to\mathbb{P}^{1} such that the open embedding of Spec⁡(B)≅𝔸2\operatorname{Spec}(B)\cong\mathbb{A}^{2} in Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) coincides with the complement of the fiber of π\pi over the infinity and π|Spec⁡(B):𝔸2→ℙ1∖{∞}=𝔸1\pi|_{\operatorname{Spec}(B)}:\mathbb{A}^{2}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{\infty\}=\mathbb{A}^{1} is one of the standard projections. Moreover, Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is a Danilov-Gizatullin surface of index three.

That Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is a Danilov-Gizatullin surface of index three, see Proposition 3.6, follows because we deduced from Proposition 2.4 that the Picard group of Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is generated by its canonical class, see Corollary 2.6. Among the Danilov-Gizatullin surfaces the only one whose Picard group is generated by the canonical class are those of index three.

We determine the explicit form of the integral closure using Wright’s explicit description of the coordinates ring of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} and Wright’s characterization of when such bundles can factorize an étale morphism of the affine plane. More precisely, we prove that if A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y] is an étale extension such that A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B and A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB, then A¯=ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]\overline{A}=\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x], where α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}, α≠0\alpha\neq 0; in particular p,q∈ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]p,q\in\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x], see Proposition 3.10. Wright noted that ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x] is a graded algebra with deg​x=−1\textrm{deg}\;x=-1 and deg​y=2\textrm{deg}\;y=2. Using this observation we show that ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x] does not contain polynomials that are regular in both variables, see Lemma 3.11. Nevertheless, we can always choose a linear automorphism that makes, for example, the polynomial pp regular in both variables, from there we arrive at the following result:

Theorem.

Suppose that A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB for every étale extension A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y]. Then every étale extension of polynomial rings ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset\mathbb{C}[x,y] is integral.

2. Étale extensions whose integral closure is a primary submodule

Recently, Rangachev proved a valuation theorem for Noetherian rings under quite general hypothesis.

Theorem 2.1.

[14, Theorem 1.1] Let A⊂BA\subset B be integral domains, suppose AA is Noetherian and BB is a finitely generated AA-algebra. Denote by A¯\overline{A} the integral closure of AA in BB. Then one of the following holds:

  • (i)

    A¯=B\overline{A}=B;

  • (ii)

    AssA¯​(B/A¯)={(0)}\mathrm{Ass}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right)=\{(0)\};

  • (iii)

    AssA¯​(B/A¯)={𝔭1,…,𝔭r}\mathrm{Ass}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right)=\{\mathfrak{p}_{1},\ldots,\mathfrak{p}_{r}\}, ht⁡(𝔭i)=1\mathrm{ht}(\mathfrak{p}_{i})=1 for all ii, and A¯=B∩(∩i=1r𝒱i)\overline{A}=B\cap\left(\cap_{i=1}^{r}\mathcal{V}_{i}\right), where 𝒱i=A¯𝔭i\mathcal{V}_{i}=\overline{A}_{\mathfrak{p}_{i}}.

Also, under the same hypothesis, he provides a description of the support of B/A¯B/\overline{A} as a closed set.

Proposition 2.2.

[14, Proposition 2.5] Assume we are in the situation of Theorem 2.1. Denote by ℐB/A¯\mathcal{I}_{B/\overline{A}} the intersection of all elements in AssA¯​(B/A¯)\mathrm{Ass}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right). Then SuppA¯​(B/A¯)=V⁡(ℐB/A¯)\mathrm{Supp}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right)=V\left(\mathcal{I}_{B/\overline{A}}\right).

We want to study the case of Theorem 2.1 where there is only one discrete valuation ring of A¯\overline{A} that does not contain BB, that is, A¯=B∩A¯𝔭\overline{A}=B\cap\overline{A}_{\mathfrak{p}}. In that situation we have the following:

Lemma 2.3.

Let A⊂BA\subset B be integral domains such that AA is Noetherian and BB is a finitely generated AA-algebra. Denote by A¯\overline{A} the integral closure of AA in BB. Suppose that A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B and Frac⁡(A¯)=Frac⁡(B)\mathrm{Frac}(\overline{A})=\mathrm{Frac}(B). Then A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB if and only if AssA¯​(B/A¯)={𝔭}\mathrm{Ass}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right)=\{\mathfrak{p}\}, ht⁡(𝔭)=1\mathrm{ht}(\mathfrak{p})=1, A¯=B∩A¯𝔭\overline{A}=B\cap\overline{A}_{\mathfrak{p}} and SuppA¯​(B/A¯)=V⁡(𝔭)\mathrm{Supp}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right)=V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right).

Proof.

As A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B, this rule out the case (i) above. We always have that AssA¯​(B/A¯)⊂SuppA¯​(B/A¯)\mathrm{Ass}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right)\subset\mathrm{Supp}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right), if AssA¯​(B/A¯)={(0)}\mathrm{Ass}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right)=\{(0)\}, then (0)∈SuppA¯​(B/A¯)(0)\in\mathrm{Supp}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right); however, this contradicts that Frac⁡(A¯)=Frac⁡(B)\mathrm{Frac}(\overline{A})=\mathrm{Frac(B)}. Then by Rangachev’s Theorem 2.1 we are left with the third possibility, that is, AssA¯​(B/A¯)={𝔭1,…,𝔭r}\mathrm{Ass}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right)=\{\mathfrak{p}_{1},\ldots,\mathfrak{p}_{r}\}, ht⁡(𝔭i)=1\mathrm{ht}(\mathfrak{p}_{i})=1, ∀i\forall i. The equivalence now follows from the definition of primary submodule [11, Definition 8.A] and Rangachev’s results. ∎

We are going to use this lemma to prove the following proposition:

Proposition 2.4.

Let kk be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Let A=k⁡[y1,…,yn]⊂B=k⁡[x1,…,xn]A=k[{y}_{1},\,\ldots,\,{y}_{n}]\subset B=k[{x}_{1},\,\ldots,\,{x}_{n}] be an étale extension of polynomial rings (each in nn indeterminates). Denote by A¯\overline{A} the integral closure of AA in BB. Suppose that A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B and that A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB. Then Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)=V⁡(𝔭)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B)=V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right), where 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is a prime ideal of height one in A¯\overline{A}, and the divisor class group Cl⁡(Spec⁡(A¯))≅ℤ≅⟨V⁡(𝔭)⟩\mathrm{Cl}(\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}))\cong\mathbb{Z}\cong\left\langle V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right)\right\rangle.

Proof.

The extension A⊂BA\subset B is étale, so it is quasi-finite and by Zariski’s Main Theorem [15, Corollaire 2, p. 42], the morphism Spec⁡(B)→Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is an open immersion. Also, the étaleness of the extension implies that Frac⁡(A)⊂Frac⁡(B)\mathrm{Frac(A)}\subset\mathrm{Frac(B)} is a finite separable algebraic extension of fields, then A¯\overline{A} is a finite module over AA, in particular A¯\overline{A} is Noetherian. It is clear that Frac⁡(A¯)=Frac⁡(B)\mathrm{Frac}(\overline{A})=\mathrm{Frac}(B).

Then the étale extension A⊂BA\subset B satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma 2.3. We are assuming that A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB, therefore, there exist a prime ideal 𝔭\mathfrak{p} of height one in A¯\overline{A} such that A¯=B∩A¯𝔭\overline{A}=B\cap\overline{A}_{\mathfrak{p}}, AssA¯​(B/A¯)={𝔭}\mathrm{Ass}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right)=\{\mathfrak{p}\}, and SuppA¯​(B/A¯)=V⁡(𝔭)\mathrm{Supp}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right)=V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right). From this we can derive the following consequences:

  • -

    Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)=V⁡(𝔭)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B)=V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right), where we identify Spec⁡(B)\operatorname{Spec}(B) with its image in Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}). In fact, denote by g:Spec⁡(B)↪Spec⁡(A¯)g:\operatorname{Spec}(B)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) the open immersion. We are going to show that Im⁡g=Spec⁡(A¯)∖SuppA¯​(B/A¯)\operatorname{Im}g=\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\mathrm{Supp}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right). Suppose that 𝔭∈Im⁡g⊂Spec⁡(A¯)\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Im}g\subset\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}), that is, there exist 𝔮∈Spec⁡(B)\mathfrak{q}\in\operatorname{Spec}(B) such that 𝔭=𝔮∩A¯\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{q}\cap\overline{A}. As gg is an open immersion we have that A¯𝔭=B𝔮=B𝔭\overline{A}_{\mathfrak{p}}=B_{\mathfrak{q}}=B_{\mathfrak{p}}, see for example [4, Exercise 2.3.9], therefore 𝔭∉SuppA¯​(B/A¯)\mathfrak{p}\notin\mathrm{Supp}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right). Conversely, suppose that 𝔭∈Spec⁡(A¯)\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) and 𝔭∉SuppA¯​(B/A¯)\mathfrak{p}\notin\mathrm{Supp}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right), that is, A¯𝔭=B𝔭\overline{A}_{\mathfrak{p}}=B_{\mathfrak{p}}. Then B⊂B𝔭=A¯𝔭B\subset B_{\mathfrak{p}}=\overline{A}_{\mathfrak{p}}, define the prime ideal 𝔯:=𝔭​A¯𝔭∩B\mathfrak{r}:=\mathfrak{p}\overline{A}_{\mathfrak{p}}\cap B, then 𝔯∈Spec⁡(B)\mathfrak{r}\in\operatorname{Spec}(B) and 𝔯∩A¯=𝔭\mathfrak{r}\cap\overline{A}=\mathfrak{p}, therefore 𝔭∈Im⁡g\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Im}g. The assertion now follows because we already know that SuppA¯​(B/A¯)=V⁡(𝔭)\mathrm{Supp}_{\overline{A}}\left(B/\overline{A}\right)=V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right).

    Cl⁡(Spec⁡(A¯))≅ℤ≅⟨V⁡(𝔭)⟩\mathrm{Cl}(\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}))\cong\mathbb{Z}\cong\left\langle V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right)\right\rangle. In fact, Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is a noetherian normal affine scheme, V⁡(𝔭)V(\mathfrak{p}) is an irreducible closed subset of codimension one, and Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)=V⁡(𝔭)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B)=V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right), then by Hartshorne [8, Chap. II, Prop.6.5] there is an exact sequence ℤ→Cl⁡(Spec⁡(A¯))→Cl⁡(Spec⁡(B))→0\mathbb{Z}\to\mathrm{Cl}(\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}))\to\mathrm{Cl}(\operatorname{Spec}(B))\to 0, where the first map is defined by 1→1⋅V⁡(𝔭)1\to 1\cdot V(\mathfrak{p}). Note that Cl⁡(Spec⁡(B))=0\mathrm{Cl}(\operatorname{Spec}(B))=0 because BB is a unique factorization domain, then Cl⁡(Spec⁡(A¯))\mathrm{Cl}(\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})) is generated by V⁡(𝔭)V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right). ∎

Suppose we are in the situation of Proposition 2.4. Then the étale morphism 𝔸n=Spec⁡(B)→𝑓𝔸n=Spec⁡(A)\mathbb{A}^{n}=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\xrightarrow{f}\mathbb{A}^{n}=\operatorname{Spec}(A) induced by the étale extension A⊂BA\subset B factorizes as f=h​gf=hg, 𝔸n=Spec⁡(B)↪𝑔Spec⁡(A¯)→ℎ𝔸n=Spec⁡(A)\mathbb{A}^{n}=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\xhookrightarrow{g}\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\xrightarrow{h}\mathbb{A}^{n}=\operatorname{Spec}(A), where gg is an open immersion and hh is finite. We denote by RhR_{h} the ramification divisor of the morphism hh, since ff is étale, we have that Rh⊂Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)=V⁡(𝔭)R_{h}\subset\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B)=V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right). By the purity of the branch locus it follows that Rh=V⁡(𝔭)R_{h}=V(\mathfrak{p}). Then we have proved:

Corollary 2.5.

Assume we are in the situation of Proposition 2.4. Then the ramification divisor Rh⊂Spec⁡(A¯)R_{h}\subset\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) of the finite morphism Spec⁡(A¯)→ℎ𝔸n=Spec⁡(A)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\xrightarrow{h}\mathbb{A}^{n}=\operatorname{Spec}(A) coincides with the prime divisor V⁡(𝔭)=Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right)=\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B).

Corollary 2.6.

Assume we are in the situation of Proposition 2.4. Suppose Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is smooth and denote by KSpec⁡(A¯)K_{\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})} its canonical divisor. Then KSpec⁡(A¯)=V⁡(𝔭)K_{\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})}=V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right), that is, the Picard group of Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is generated by the canonical class.

Proof.

We have that KSpec⁡(A¯)=h∗​(K𝔸2)+RhK_{\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})}=h^{*}(K_{\mathbb{A}^{2}})+R_{h} by the ramification formula [9, Theorem 5.5] applied to the dominant morphism Spec⁡(A¯)→ℎ𝔸2=Spec⁡(A)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\xrightarrow{h}\mathbb{A}^{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(A). Then KSpec⁡(A¯)=RhK_{\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})}=R_{h}. The conclusion now follows from Corollary 2.5. ∎

3. Two-dimensional étale extensions

In this section k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}, the field of complex numbers. We are going to apply Proposition 2.4 to carry out Wright’s geometric approach for two-dimensional non-integral étale extensions [18] in the case A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB. Wright proved that if we start with an étale extension A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y] that is not integral, it is possible to construct a normal affine variety that admits the structure of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, more precisely:

Theorem 3.1.

[18, Theorem 4.3] Let A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y] be an étale extension such that A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B, then there exist a normal affine variety VV containing U=𝔸2U=\mathbb{A}^{2} as an open subvariety having the following properties:

  • i)

    F=V∖UF=V\setminus U is a rational curve whose normalization is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} and each singular point of FF has one-point desingularization.

  • ii)

    there is a map π:V→ℙ1\pi:V\to\mathbb{P}^{1} such that FF is the set-theoretic fiber of a point z∈ℙ1z\in\mathbb{P}^{1}, and the restriction map π|U:U→ℙ1∖{z}=𝔸1\pi|_{U}:U\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{z\}=\mathbb{A}^{1} is the projection onto a coordinate line.

  • iii)

    there is a map f:V→𝔸2f:V\to\mathbb{A}^{2} such that f|Uf|_{U} is étale.

Moreover, if we assume that A¯\overline{A} is smooth, then VV can be chosen to be smooth and F≅𝔸1F\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}. Even more, [18, Remark p. 605] if FF has multiplicity one in the fiber, that is, π−1​(z)=𝔸1\pi^{-1}(z)=\mathbb{A}^{1} scheme-theoretically, then VV is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} via the map π:V→ℙ1\pi:V\to\mathbb{P}^{1}.

In order to get an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} we first need to prove that the integral closure is smooth. We are going to show that this is the case if A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB. To achieve this we apply the following result of Gurjar and Miyanishi. In fact, the specific case we need from this result, that is, when X=𝔸2X=\mathbb{A}^{2}, was proved by Miyanishi in [13, Chap. I, Sect. 6].

Theorem 3.2.

[7, Theorem 1] Let φ:Xu→Xl\varphi:X_{u}\to X_{l} be an étale morphism, where Xu=XX_{u}=X and Xl=XX_{l}=X are two copies of an irreducible normal affine surface XX defined over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Let X~\widetilde{X} be the normalization of XlX_{l} in the function field of XuX_{u}. Then X~∖Xu\widetilde{X}\setminus X_{u} is a disjoint union of irreducible curves CiC_{i}, each of which is isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}. Further, each singularity of X~\widetilde{X} which is not contained in XuX_{u} is a cyclic quotient singularity. Any irreducible component of X~∖Xu\widetilde{X}\setminus X_{u} contains at most one such singular point.

Consider now an étale extension A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y], or equivalently, the corresponding étale morphism f=(p,q):𝔸2=Spec⁡(B)→𝔸2=Spec⁡(A)f=(p,q):\mathbb{A}^{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\mathbb{A}^{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(A). Suppose that A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B and that A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB, by Proposition 2.4 we have that Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)=V⁡(𝔭)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B)=V\left(\mathfrak{p}\right) is reduced and irreducible. Applying the Gurjar-Miyanishi’s Theorem 3.2 to the morphism f=(p,q):𝔸2=Spec⁡(B)→𝔸2=Spec⁡(A)f=(p,q):\mathbb{A}^{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\mathbb{A}^{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(A) implies that Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)≅𝔸1\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B)\cong\mathbb{A}^{1} scheme-theoretically, and consequently Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) has no singularities at all. We have proved the following:

Proposition 3.3.

Let A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y] be an étale extension of polynomial rings. Denote by A¯\overline{A} the integral closure of AA in BB. Suppose that A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB. Then A¯\overline{A} is a smooth ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra.

Under the hypothesis that A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB it follows now from Wright’s construction that the variety VV in Wright’s Theorem 3.1 is exactly Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}), and it admits a map to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} making it an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle except over one point of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} whose fiber is exactly F=Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)≅𝔸1F=\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B)\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}, now scheme-theoretically. Therefore, we have proved that Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) has the structure of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, such that the open embedding of Spec⁡(B)≅𝔸2\operatorname{Spec}(B)\cong\mathbb{A}^{2} in Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) coincides with the complement of the fiber of π\pi over the infinity and π|Spec⁡(B):𝔸2→ℙ1∖{∞}=𝔸1\pi|_{\operatorname{Spec}(B)}:\mathbb{A}^{2}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{\infty\}=\mathbb{A}^{1} is one of the standard projections. Nevertheless, we must make the following observation:

Remark 3.4.

In his Theorem 3.1, Wright assumed that the curves p=0p=0 and q=0q=0 each have two points at infinity in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} that coincide with the points at infinity on the lines x=0x=0 and y=0y=0. He need this in his proof to accommodate the variety VV within the blowups performed in the resolution of the birational map associated to the étale extension. It is always possible to make such an assumption at the cost of modifying the original étale extension. Its means that if we start with an arbitrary non-integral étale extension A⊂BA\subset B, then we probably need to change to a different non-integral étale extension A′⊂B′A^{\prime}\subset B^{\prime} by means of an automorphism, if we want to construct VV from Spec⁡(A′¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A^{\prime}}) as Wright does.

Let’s prove using Proposition 2.4 that when A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB, we don’t need to make Wright’s assumptions. Proving it this way will be useful later to explicitly describe the integral closure and to prove Theorem 3.12.

Theorem 3.5.

Let A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y] be an étale extension such that A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B and A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB, then Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is a smooth affine surface that admits the structure of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, π:Spec⁡(A¯)→ℙ1\pi:\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\to\mathbb{P}^{1} such that the open embedding of Spec⁡(B)≅𝔸2\operatorname{Spec}(B)\cong\mathbb{A}^{2} in Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) coincides with the complement of the fiber of π\pi over the infinity and π|Spec⁡(B):𝔸2→ℙ1∖{∞}=𝔸1\pi|_{\operatorname{Spec}(B)}:\mathbb{A}^{2}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{\infty\}=\mathbb{A}^{1} is one of the standard projections.

Proof.

By Proposition 2.4 and Proposition 3.3 we have that Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is a smooth affine surface such that Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)≅𝔸1\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B)\cong\mathbb{A}^{1} scheme-theoretically, lets denote this affine line by F:=Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)F:=\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B). On the other hand, Spec⁡(B)≅𝔸2\operatorname{Spec}(B)\cong\mathbb{A}^{2} admits two 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations over 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} given by the standard projections πi:Spec⁡(B)→𝔸1\pi_{i}:\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\mathbb{A}^{1}, i=1,2i=1,2, corresponding to the containments ℂ⁡[x]⊂ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x]\subset\mathbb{C}[x,y] and ℂ⁡[y]⊂ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[y]\subset\mathbb{C}[x,y] respectively. It is known [13, Chap. I, Lemma 4.3 ] that each πi\pi_{i} extends to an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration π~i:Spec⁡(A¯)→C\widetilde{\pi}_{i}:\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\to C where C≅𝔸1C\cong\mathbb{A}^{1} or C≅ℙ1C\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}.

We are going to argue as in [6, Lemma 5.2] to show that at least one of the πi\pi_{i}’s extends to an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. Suppose that both fibrations π1\pi_{1} and π2\pi_{2} extends to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations over 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}, that is, π~1:Spec⁡(A¯)→Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[x])\widetilde{\pi}_{1}:\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\to\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x]) and π~2:Spec⁡(A¯)→Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[y])\widetilde{\pi}_{2}:\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\to\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[y]). Then FF is contained in some fiber of π~1\widetilde{\pi}_{1} and in some fiber of π~2\widetilde{\pi}_{2}. This means that xx and yy are constant along FF. Therefore, any function f∈Γ⁡(Spec⁡(A¯),𝒪Spec⁡(A¯))⊂Γ⁡(Spec⁡(B),𝒪Spec⁡(B))=ℂ⁡[x,y]f\in\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}),\mathcal{O}_{\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})})\subset\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}(B),\mathcal{O}_{\operatorname{Spec}(B)})=\mathbb{C}[x,y] is also constant along FF. This leads to a contradiction, because given any two points of FF there is a regular function of Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) that separates them.

Then at least one of the πi\pi_{i}’s extends to an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. Without loss of generality, suppose that it is π1\pi_{1} that extends to an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration π~1:Spec⁡(A¯)→ℙ1\widetilde{\pi}_{1}:\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\to\mathbb{P}^{1}. Then π~1−1​(∞)=Spec⁡(A¯)∖Spec⁡(B)≅𝔸1\widetilde{\pi}_{1}^{-1}(\infty)=\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(B)\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}, scheme-theoretically. Therefore, π~1\widetilde{\pi}_{1} is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} that satisfies the desired properties. ∎

It is known that every 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle π:V→ℙ1\pi:V\to\mathbb{P}^{1}, where VV is a affine nonsingular surface, can be realized as the complement V=𝔽n∖SV=\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus S of an ample section SS, where 𝔽n=ℙ⁡(𝒪ℙ1⊕𝒪ℙ1​(−n))\mathbb{F}_{n}=\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-n)\right), n≥0n\geq 0, is a Hirzebruch surface, and the canonical projection π~n:𝔽n→ℙ1\tilde{\pi}_{n}:\mathbb{F}_{n}\to\mathbb{P}^{1} extends π\pi. In this case, S=C0+12​(S2+n)​FS=C_{0}+\frac{1}{2}(S^{2}+n)F, where C0C_{0} is a section of π~n\tilde{\pi}_{n} with self-intersection C02=−nC_{0}^{2}=-n, FF is a fiber of π~n\tilde{\pi}_{n}, and S2≥n+2S^{2}\geq n+2. Moreover, nn and S2S^{2} are uniquely determined by VV and π\pi, see [3], [12, Lemma 5.5.1], [18, Theorem 2.3].

Danilov and Gizatullin proved that the isomorphism class of the complement V=𝔽n∖SV=\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus S of an ample section SS in a Hirzebruch surface 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n} depends only on the self-intersection number S2S^{2} and neither on nn nor on the choice of the section SS, see [3, Theorem 5.8.1], [2, Corollary 4.8]. These affine surfaces VV are called Danilov-Gizatullin surfaces of index S2S^{2}.

The Picard group of the Hirzebruch surface 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n} is Pic⁡(𝔽n)≅ℤ2\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbb{F}_{n})\cong\mathbb{Z}^{2}, freely generated by the class of C0C_{0} and the class of a fiber FF of π~n\tilde{\pi}_{n}, and C02=−nC_{0}^{2}=-n, F2=0F^{2}=0 and C0​F=1C_{0}F=1. The canonical divisor is given by K𝔽n=−2​C0−(n+2)​F=−2​S+(S2−2)​FK_{\mathbb{F}_{n}}=-2C_{0}-(n+2)F=-2S+(S^{2}-2)F. Therefore, the Picard group of the Danilov-Gizatullin surface 𝔽n∖S\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus S is freely generated by the class of F|𝔽n∖SF|_{\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus S}, Pic⁡(𝔽n∖S)≅ℤ\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus S)\cong\mathbb{Z}, and the canonical divisor is given by K𝔽n∖S=(S2−2)​F|𝔽n∖SK_{\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus S}=(S^{2}-2)F|_{\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus S}.

Proposition 3.6.

Let A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y] be an étale extension such that A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B and A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB, then Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is a Danilov-Gizatullin surface of index 3.

Proof.

It follows from Theorem 3.5 that Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. By the observations above it is in particular a Danilov-Gizatullin surface Spec⁡(A¯)≅𝔽n∖S\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})\cong\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus S. On the other hand, we know by Corollary 2.6 that the Picard group of Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) is generated by the canonical divisor KSpec⁡(A¯)K_{\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A})}. It follows that (S2−2)​F|𝔽n∖S=F|𝔽n∖S(S^{2}-2)F|_{\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus S}=F|_{\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus S}, this forces S2=3S^{2}=3. ∎

Now, the problem is whether a Danilov-Gizatullin surface (equivalently, an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}) can factorizes an étale morphism of the complex affine plane. This is precisely the situation Wright conjectured should not happen. Geometric Formulation of Wright’s conjecture: let VV be an affine variety which is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, U=V∖FU=V\setminus F, where FF is a fiber in VV. There does not exist f:V→𝔸2f:V\to\mathbb{A}^{2} such that f|Uf|_{U} is étale, [18, Conjecture 3.2].

To address his conjecture, Wright provides an explicit description of the coordinate ring of an affine 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, that is, he describes Γ⁡(V)\Gamma(V) as a subring of ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y], corresponding to the containment of U≅𝔸2U\cong\mathbb{A}^{2} in VV. Let’s recall his construction.

Theorem 3.7.

[18, Theorem 3.1] Let VV be an affine variety which is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} with structure map π:V→ℙ1\pi:V\to\mathbb{P}^{1}. Pick xx such that the function field of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} is ℂ⁡(x)\mathbb{C}(x), and let U0=π−1​(Spec⁡ℂ⁡[x])U_{0}=\pi^{-1}\left(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{C}[x]\right), U1=π−1​(Spec⁡ℂ⁡[x−1])U_{1}=\pi^{-1}\left(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{C}[x^{-1}]\right). Then V=U0∪U1V=U_{0}\cup U_{1} and there exist y∈Γ⁡(V)y\in\Gamma(V) such that U0=Spec⁡ℂ⁡[x,y]U_{0}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{C}[x,y], U1=Spec⁡ℂ⁡[x′,y′]U_{1}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{C}[x^{\prime},y^{\prime}] where

x′=x−1,y′=xm​y+α1​xm−1+α2​xm−2+⋯+αm−1​x,\displaystyle x^{\prime}=x^{-1},\quad y^{\prime}=x^{m}y+\alpha_{1}x^{m-1}+\alpha_{2}x^{m-2}+\cdots+\alpha_{m-1}x,

where m≥2m\geq 2 and α1,…,αm−1∈ℂ\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{m-1}\in\mathbb{C} not all zero. Moreover

Γ⁡(V)=ℂ⁡[t0,t1,…,tm],\displaystyle\Gamma(V)=\mathbb{C}[t_{0},t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}],

where

t0\displaystyle t_{0} =y,\displaystyle=y, (3.1)
t1\displaystyle t_{1} =x​y,\displaystyle=xy,
t2\displaystyle t_{2} =x2​y+α1​x,\displaystyle=x^{2}y+\alpha_{1}x,
t3\displaystyle t_{3} =x3​y+α1​x2+α2​x,\displaystyle=x^{3}y+\alpha_{1}x^{2}+\alpha_{2}x,
…\displaystyle\ldots
tm\displaystyle t_{m} =xm​y+α1​xm−1+α2​xm−2+⋯+αm−1​x(=y′).\displaystyle=x^{m}y+\alpha_{1}x^{m-1}+\alpha_{2}x^{m-2}+\cdots+\alpha_{m-1}x\;(=y^{\prime}).

Conversely, every ring of the form ℂ⁡[t0,t1,…,tm]\mathbb{C}[t_{0},t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}] above can be made into the coordinate ring of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}.

In view of this description, Wright’s conjecture can be rephrased as follows. Algebraic formulation of Wright’s conjecture: there does not exist a pair of polynomials p,q∈ℂ⁡[t0,t1,…,tm]⊂ℂ⁡[x,y]p,q\in\mathbb{C}[t_{0},t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}]\subset\mathbb{C}[x,y], where t0,t1,…,tmt_{0},t_{1},\ldots,t_{m} are as in (3.1) (α1,…,αm−1∈ℂ\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{m-1}\in\mathbb{C} not all zero), with ∂(p,q)∂(x,y)\frac{\partial(p,q)}{\partial(x,y)} non-vanishing (i.e., constant) on 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}, [18, Conjecture 3.2].

Remark 3.8.

The number of generators of the algebra Γ⁡(V)\Gamma(V), that is, the integer m+1m+1, is completely determined by the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle π:V→ℙ1\pi:V\to\mathbb{P}^{1}. In fact, let V=𝔽n∖SV=\mathbb{F}_{n}\setminus S be the corresponding Danilov-Gizatullin surface, then m=S2m=S^{2}, see [18, p. 599, above the Conjecture 3.2] and [2, Proposition 3.5].

Wright succeeded in proving the following case of his conjecture.

Theorem 3.9.

[18, Theorem 3.3] Wright’s conjecture is true in the case where the coefficient α1\alpha_{1} is non-zero.

Putting together the previous results we obtain the following explicit description of the integral closure of a non-integral étale extension whose integral closure is primary.

Proposition 3.10.

Let A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y] be an étale extension such that A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B and A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB, then A¯=ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]\overline{A}=\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x], where α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}, α≠0\alpha\neq 0. In particular p,q∈ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]p,q\in\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x].

Proof.

By Theorem 3.5 we have that V=Spec⁡(A¯)V=\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) admits the structure of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} such that the open embedding of Spec⁡(B)≅𝔸2\operatorname{Spec}(B)\cong\mathbb{A}^{2} in Spec⁡(A¯)\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{A}) coincides with the complement of the fiber over the infinity and π|Spec⁡(B):𝔸2→ℙ1∖{∞}=𝔸1\pi|_{\operatorname{Spec}(B)}:\mathbb{A}^{2}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{\infty\}=\mathbb{A}^{1} is one of the standard projections. Moreover, in Proposition 3.6 we proved that VV is a Danilov-Gizatullin surface of index 3, therefore, m=3m=3 by Remark 3.8. It now follows from Wright’s Theorem 3.7 that p,q∈Γ⁡(V)=ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y+α1​x,x3​y+α1​x2+α2​x]p,q\in\Gamma(V)=\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y+\alpha_{1}x,x^{3}y+\alpha_{1}x^{2}+\alpha_{2}x], where α1,α2∈ℂ\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in\mathbb{C} cannot be both zero. By Wright’s Theorem 3.9 we have that α1=0\alpha_{1}=0. ∎

At this point we are left with the following case of Wright’s conjecture: there does not exist a pair of polynomials p,q∈ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]p,q\in\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x], α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}, α≠0\alpha\neq 0 such that ∂(p,q)∂(x,y)\frac{\partial(p,q)}{\partial(x,y)} is constant. This is precisely the simplest unknown case of Wright’s conjecture [18, pag. 601]. We are going to use Proposition 3.10 and Wright’s observation that ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x] is a graded algebra with deg​x=−1\textrm{deg}\;x=-1 and deg​y=2\textrm{deg}\;y=2 to prove that if it is always the case that A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB then every two-dimensional étale extension is integral.

With respect to this grading the generators of ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x] have degrees: deg​y=2\textrm{deg}\;y=2, deg​x​y=1,deg​x2​y=0\textrm{deg}\;xy=1,\textrm{deg}\;x^{2}y=0 and deg​(x3​y+α​x)=−1\textrm{deg}\;(x^{3}y+\alpha x)=-1. Let f⁡(x,y)∈ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]f(x,y)\in\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x] be a homogeneous polynomial of weighted degree −m<0-m<0. We can write:

f⁡(x,y)\displaystyle f(x,y) =∑2​l1+l2−l4=−mfl1​l2​l3​l4​yl1​(x​y)l2​(x2​y)l3​(x3​y+α​x)l4,li∈ℤ≥0,fl1​l2​l3​l4∈ℂ,\displaystyle=\sum_{2l_{1}+l_{2}-l_{4}=-m}f_{l_{1}l_{2}l_{3}l_{4}}y^{l_{1}}(xy)^{l_{2}}(x^{2}y)^{l_{3}}(x^{3}y+\alpha x)^{l_{4}},\quad\quad l_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},\quad f_{l_{1}l_{2}l_{3}l_{4}}\in\mathbb{C},
f⁡(x,y)\displaystyle f(x,y) =∑2​l1+l2−l4=−mfl1​l2​l3​l4​yl1​(x​y)l2​(x2​y)l3​(x3​y+α​x)2​l1+l2+m,\displaystyle=\sum_{2l_{1}+l_{2}-l_{4}=-m}f_{l_{1}l_{2}l_{3}l_{4}}y^{l_{1}}(xy)^{l_{2}}(x^{2}y)^{l_{3}}(x^{3}y+\alpha x)^{2l_{1}+l_{2}+m},
f⁡(x,y)\displaystyle f(x,y) =(x3​y+α​x)m​∑2​l1+l2−l4=−mfl1​l2​l3​l4​(x6​y3+2​α​x4​y2+α2​x2​y)l1​(x4​y2+α​x2​y)l2​(x2​y)l3,\displaystyle=(x^{3}y+\alpha x)^{m}\sum_{2l_{1}+l_{2}-l_{4}=-m}f_{l_{1}l_{2}l_{3}l_{4}}(x^{6}y^{3}+2\alpha x^{4}y^{2}+\alpha^{2}x^{2}y)^{l_{1}}(x^{4}y^{2}+\alpha x^{2}y)^{l_{2}}(x^{2}y)^{l_{3}},

then f⁡(x,y)=(x3​y+α​x)m​g​(z)f(x,y)=(x^{3}y+\alpha x)^{m}g(z), where g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] and z=x2​yz=x^{2}y.

For the next definition, let’s consider the usual grading, that is, deg​x=1\textrm{deg}\;x=1 and deg​y=1\textrm{deg}\;y=1. We say a polynomial p⁡(x,y)∈ℂ⁡[x,y]p(x,y)\in\mathbb{C}[x,y] of total degree nn is regular in xx if it contains a term in xnx^{n}. It is well known that for any polynomial p⁡(x,y)p(x,y) it is always possible to find an invertible linear transformation x=a​v+b​wx=av+bw, y=c​v+d​wy=cv+dw, (a,b,c,d∈ℂa,b,c,d\in\mathbb{C}, a​d−c​d≠0ad-cd\neq 0) such that r⁡(v,w)=p⁡(a​v+b​w,c​v+d​w)r(v,w)=p(av+bw,cv+dw) is regular in vv and ww, see [10, (2.7), p. 5].

Lemma 3.11.

The algebra ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x], α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}, α≠0\alpha\neq 0 does not contain polynomials that are regular in both variables.

Proof.

Suppose p⁡(x,y)∈ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]p(x,y)\in\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x] is a polynomial of total (usual) degree nn that is regular in both variables. Then in particular p⁡(x,y)p(x,y) contains a term in xnx^{n} and consequently p⁡(x,y)p(x,y) has a non-zero homogeneous component of weighted degree −n<0-n<0. On the other hand, we already observe that all homogeneous polynomials of weighted degree −n<0-n<0 in ℂ⁡[y,x​y,x2​y,x3​y+α​x]\mathbb{C}[y,xy,x^{2}y,x^{3}y+\alpha x] are of the form f⁡(x,y)=(x3​y+α​x)n​g​(z)f(x,y)=(x^{3}y+\alpha x)^{n}g(z), where g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] and z=x2​yz=x^{2}y. This is a contradiction because p⁡(x,y)p(x,y) is a polynomial of total (usual) degree nn. ∎

Theorem 3.12.

Suppose that A¯\overline{A} is a primary A¯\overline{A}-submodule of BB for every étale extension A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y]. Then every étale extension of polynomial rings ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset\mathbb{C}[x,y] is integral.

Proof.

Suppose that there exist an étale extension A=ℂ⁡[p,q]⊂B=ℂ⁡[x,y]A=\mathbb{C}[p,q]\subset B=\mathbb{C}[x,y] that is not integral, that is, A¯≠B\overline{A}\neq B (equivalently the corresponding étale morphism (p,q):𝔸2=Spec⁡(B)→𝔸2=Spec⁡(A)(p,q):\mathbb{A}^{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\mathbb{A}^{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(A) is not injective, [16, Theorem 46]). Choose an invertible linear substitution x=a​v+b​wx=av+bw, y=c​v+d​wy=cv+dw, (a,b,c,d∈ℂa,b,c,d\in\mathbb{C}, a​d−c​d≠0ad-cd\neq 0) such that r⁡(v,w)=p⁡(a​v+b​w,c​v+d​w)r(v,w)=p(av+bw,cv+dw) is regular in both variables vv and ww. After composing the morphism (p,q)(p,q) with this linear automorphism we obtain another étale extension ℂ⁡[r,s]⊂ℂ⁡[v,w]\mathbb{C}[r,s]\subset\mathbb{C}[v,w] that is also non-integral (equivalently an étale morphism (r,s):𝔸2=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[v,w])→𝔸2=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[r,s])(r,s):\mathbb{A}^{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[v,w])\to\mathbb{A}^{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[r,s]) that is not injective), where r⁡(v,w)=p⁡(a​v+b​w,c​v+d​w)r(v,w)=p(av+bw,cv+dw) and s⁡(v,w)=q⁡(a​v+b​w,c​v+d​w)s(v,w)=q(av+bw,cv+dw). By hypothesis we have that ℂ⁡[r,s]¯\overline{\mathbb{C}[r,s]} is a primary ℂ⁡[r,s]¯\overline{\mathbb{C}[r,s]}-submodule of ℂ⁡[v,w]\mathbb{C}[v,w], applying Proposition 3.10 to the non-integral étale extension ℂ⁡[r,s]⊂ℂ⁡[v,w]\mathbb{C}[r,s]\subset\mathbb{C}[v,w] we have that r,s∈ℂ⁡[w,v​w,v2​w,v3​w+β​v]r,s\in\mathbb{C}[w,vw,v^{2}w,v^{3}w+\beta v], where β∈ℂ\beta\in\mathbb{C}, β≠0\beta\neq 0. By construction the polynomial rr is regular in vv and ww, however, by Lemma 3.11 the algebra ℂ⁡[w,v​w,v2​w,v3​w+β​v]\mathbb{C}[w,vw,v^{2}w,v^{3}w+\beta v] does not contain polynomials regular in both variables, a contradiction. Hence A¯=B\overline{A}=B. ∎
